item.content:encoded:
Several cool things have happened here:

  • Almost all GoIs (at least those present at time of original writing) are addressed in a single article.
  • We have more ORIA politics.
  • It shows that ORIA format can go beyond the "anomalous item profile/report" that the Foundation/GOC/Herman Fuller/MCF/MC&D etc. cannot do. Not all ORIA format articles have to be reports on various anomalous objects; they can even be trade disputes (only more interesting than George Lucas' interpretation of "trade disputes").

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Well, the way I figured it, most of the Groups of Interest are worth paying interest to because they have some kind of global or large-scale influence; otherwise, they'd just be anomalous and the Foundation could absorb/contain/suppress/amnesticize their membership, which would probably be their MO for all these groups if they could get away with it.

Now, I won't deny that all of the GoIs being involved in this particular year's roundup is the most plausible thing in the world, rather than a fun exercise in seeing how to make all the jigsaw pieces fall into place; and for that reason, I get that it's not everyone's bag. But given that this iteration of ORIA is active throughout the entire Muslim-majority world, there's a much bigger net to cover than just Tehran.

item.content:encoded:
+ way too much info
- I'm so smart, right?

[In the story, most of the groups aren't in Iran, and some aren't even in the middle east. They're just inside the ORIA's sphere of influence. In the tale, they mention people captured in Pakistan, Tunisia (which is in Africa,) Oman, Afghanistan, and East Jerusalem, which is a pretty big sphere of influence.

Someone will probably bring up the point how Iran can capture people in other nations. The things is, many of the above mentioned areas are also Islamic, and may take offense at foreign organizations taking bizarre and possibly dangerous artifacts out of their country. So while they do not openly support Iran, they may turn a blind eye to the capturing of foreign agents, especially if they are of religious nature. For example, Saudi Arabia bans christian missionaries from working in it. What would they think of a CotBG cultist? Besides which, the ORIA isn't stationing battalions of soldiers all the time. Most of the captures are probably by small teams, which are easier to tolerate.

Finally, Iran can probably get its teams in using anomalous artifacts. This can also explain how AWCY, Prometheus labs, Dr. Wondertainment's agents and the Serpent's Hand got in.

As for MC&D, they can just Bribe their way in to any country]

item.content:encoded:
This notion that every single GoI is so internationally widespread and so numerous that multiple personnel are captured by ORIA on an annual basis doesn't make a whole lot of sense to me.

This sort of encapsulates my issues with GoIs, actually. The level of anomalous activity that would need to be going on to make this scenario plausible would be completely unable to be covered up in any meaningful way, in which case why is any of this secret, or even considered "anomalous"? Toymakers, hipsters, magic hillbillies, clowns, the United Nations, industrial laboratories, United States federal agents and god knows who else are running amok in the streets of Tehran (and I assume everywhere else in the world), operating on mutable principles of reality that can be discarded at will.

The world in which this story occurs strikes me as essentially an ongoing real-life Looney Toons short. Which, you know, more power to the people who like that sort of thing, but it's definitely not for me.
